extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing whether references (publications, patents, drawings, applications, sales, etc.) qualify as prior art and how such references may be used to reject claims under novelty (35 U.S.C. 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103). Includes special-topic rules (e.g., tax strategies, drawings, secret patents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign sale + publication can create pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) statutory bar
rubrics_metrics.description: When (i) a publication identifies the plant, (ii) a foreign sale occurs that puts one of ordinary skill in the art in possession of the plant itself, and (iii) such possession permits asexual reproduction of the plant without undue experimentation by one of ordinary skill in the art, that combination of facts constitutes a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) statutory bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board/court may remand for fact-finding to determine whether foreign sales were accessible to the skilled artisan and whether the skilled artisan could have reproduced the plant asexually without undue experimentation. See MPEP § 2152.02(d) for foreign-sales prior art under AIA first-inventor-to-file provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures/drawings may constitute an enabling disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and thus may be used to reject claims to the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The picture must show all the claimed structural features and how they are put together. Drawings can constitute description for anticipation 'by drawings alone as well as by words.' See In re Bager and MPEP § 2125 (drawings as prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility need not be disclosed in a reference for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute anticipatory prior art, a reference must identically disclose the claimed compound, but no utility need be disclosed by the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of efficacy or disclosed use is not required for a reference to be enabling or anticipatory of a claim to an old compound. See In re Schoenwald and related Federal Circuit decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are prior art for all they contain
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent reference is relevant not only for what the patentee emphasizes as their invention but for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one of ordinary skill in the art, including nonpreferred embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of patents as references is not limited to patentees' descriptions; optional or nonpreferred embodiments disclosed in a patent can teach the claimed subject matter and may be relied upon even if the reference 'teaches away.' See In re Heck, Merck & Co. v. Biocraft Labs., and related cases; see MPEP §§ 2131.05 and 2145 (teaching away discussions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpreferred and alternative embodiments can be used as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosed examples and preferred embodiments do not constitute a teaching away from broader disclosures or nonpreferred embodiments; disclosure of more than one alternative does not teach away from any of those alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that a reference 'teaches away' by showing an embodiment as inferior are insufficient where there is no discovery beyond what was known in the art. See In re Susi, In re Gurley, and In re Fulton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later factual references can sometimes be relied on even if they postdate filing
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain circumstances, references cited to show a universal fact need not be available as prior art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; later publications may be cited to show facts such as that undue experimentation would have been required, a parameter was critical or not, a specification statement was inaccurate, inoperation or lack of utility, or indefiniteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such post-effective-filing-date factual evidence may be used to illuminate specific factual questions (e.g., enablement, criticality) but it is impermissible to use later factual references to determine whether the application met the written-description or enablement requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) as of the filing date. See In re Wilson, Corneil, Rainer, Marzocchi, Langer, Koller, and Amgen v. Sanofi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategies are treated as prior art under AIA section 14
rubrics_metrics.description: For novelty and nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, any strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability (a 'tax strategy') shall be deemed insufficient to differentiate a claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'tax liability' covers liabilities under federal, state, local, or foreign law. The provision took effect Sept 16, 2011 and applies to applications pending or filed on/after that date and patents issued on/after that date. There are two statutory exclusions (see next rubric entries). Examiner treatment parallels printed-matter limitations (MPEP § 2112.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions to AIA section 14 (tax strategy provision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two exclusions: (1) the provision does not apply to that part of an invention that is a method, apparatus, technology, computer program product, or system used solely for preparing a tax or information return or other tax filing (including recording/transmitting/organizing data related to such filing); (2) the provision does not apply to that part that is used solely for financial management, to the extent it is severable from any tax strategy or does not limit the use of any tax strategy by any taxpayer or advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim limitations fall within these exclusions (e.g., software solely enabling tax filing), such limitations may be given patentable weight; otherwise limitations directed to a tax strategy must be treated as within the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure for claims relating to tax strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining claims related to tax strategies, follow a procedure: construe the claim per MPEP § 2111 et seq., analyze 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 in accordance with current guidance (unaffected by sec. 14), identify any limitations relating to a tax strategy (noting exclusions), and evaluate the claim for 102/103 treating tax-strategy limitations as within the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.06.01 may be used to indicate claim limitations interpreted as tax strategies. Treating tax-strategy limitations as within the prior art is analogous to treatment of printed-matter limitations (MPEP § 2112.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.06.01 wording for tax-strategy limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Template paragraph to indicate a claim limitation interpreted as a tax strategy is being treated as within the prior art and insufficient to differentiate the claim from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes Examiner Note instructing to recite the claim limitation in bracket 1 and insert claim numbers in bracket 2; see MPEP § 2124.01 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of computer-implemented methods involving tax strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-implemented method that is novel and non-obvious is not affected by the tax-strategy provision even if used for a tax purpose; however, a prior-art computer-implemented method does not become non-obvious merely by implementing a novel tax strategy. Claim limitations solely directed to enabling tax filing or to financial management (when severable) should be given patentable weight; limitations directed to a tax strategy should not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze claims for 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 as usual; do not give patentable weight to tax-strategy limitations for purposes of 102/103 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and pictures as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure which is claimed; origin of the drawing is immaterial and unintended or unexplained features in a utility patent drawing can still be relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose and suggest to one of ordinary skill in the art. See In re Mraz and In re Aslanian; see MPEP § 2121.04 for drawings as 'enabled disclosures.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions in drawings are not evidence of actual proportions when drawings are not to scale
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference does not disclose that drawings are to scale and is silent as to dimensions, arguments based on measurement of drawing features have little evidentiary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drawings are not to scale, measurements from them are unreliable; however, the description in combination with the drawings can be relied upon to determine what the reference reasonably teaches. See Hockerson-Halberstadt and In re Wright examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: The name 'patent' alone does not make a document available as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: What a foreign country designates to be a patent may not make the document available as prior art for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre-AIA 102(a)/(b); substance of the rights conferred and how information is controlled are determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret patents insufficiently accessible to the public are not 'printed publications' and thus not prior art under 102(a)/(b) until they are public. A document must be at least minimally available (laid open, disseminated in printed form, etc.) to constitute prior art. However, for pre-AIA 102(d) rejections, secret patents may be usable as of grant date in some circumstances. See In re Ekenstam, In re Carlson, In re Kathawala and MPEP §§ 2126–2135 discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date foreign patent is effective as a reference is usually patent grant date
rubrics_metrics.description: The date a patent is available as a reference is generally the date the patent rights are formally awarded (the date the sovereign bestows patent rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an exception when the patent is secret as of the date rights are awarded. Examiners may consult MPEP § 901.05 for dates of patenting for many foreign patents and case law lists (e.g., In re Monks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of a patent reference that is a 'patent' but not a 'publication' — use of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patented document is used as a patent (not as a publication), the examiner may rely on any information provided in the specification which relates to the subject matter of the patented claims when making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre-AIA 102(a),(b) or (d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed details in the specification germane to the claimed invention can be relied upon; courts have held that 'invention ... patented' includes all disclosed aspects. See Ex parte Ovist, In re Kathawala. Note In re Fuge's limited holding ('at the least, the scope ... embraces everything included in the claim').

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned patent applications disclosed to the public can be prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned patent application may become evidence of prior art only when it has been appropriately disclosed (e.g., referenced in a patent disclosure, published, or voluntarily disclosed). It becomes available as prior art as of the date the public gains access to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter of an abandoned application referred to in a prior-art U.S. patent or application publication may be relied upon in a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102(e) rejection based on that patent or application publication if the disclosure is actually included or incorporated by reference. See Lee Pharmaceutical v. Kreps and In re Lund examples; consult MPEP § 901.02 and §§ 2136/2154 for priority-date issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canceled matter in applications and how it affects rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Canceled matter in an application file of a U.S. patent or application publication cannot be relied upon in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102(e); canceled matter only becomes available as prior art as of the date the application file history is available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such canceled matter may, however, be available as prior art under other subsections (e.g., 102(a)(1) or pre-AIA 102(b)) depending on public availability. See Ex Parte Stalego and In re Lund; see MPEP §§ 2136.02, 2154 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laid open foreign applications may constitute 'printed publications' depending on accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When a foreign application's specification is laid open for public inspection or announced in an official journal such that anyone can inspect or obtain copies, it may be sufficiently accessible to be a 'printed publication' under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or pre-AIA 102(a)/(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a laid open application constitutes a 'publication' depends on accessibility. Technological reproduction and distribution increase accessibility (e.g., microfilm, diazo copies distributed to suboffices). Examiners should confirm the date of publication via review of a copy. See In re Wyer and MPEP § 901.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending U.S. applications confidentiality and when they can be relied on
rubrics_metrics.description: All pending U.S. patent applications are preserved in confidence except for published applications, reissue applications, and applications opened to public inspection. If an unpublished application shares an assignee or at least one inventor in common with the application being examined, rejections may be proper in certain circumstances (e.g., provisional double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims between applications are not independent or distinct, provisional double patenting rejections or provisional rejections under 102(a)(2)/pre-AIA 102(e) or 103 may be appropriate in copending situations. See 37 CFR 1.14(a), MPEP § 804 and §§ 2136.01, 2146.03(a), 2154.01(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and legal standard for 'printed publication' (public accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a 'printed publication' if it is accessible to the public — i.e., it has been disseminated or otherwise made available to the extent that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is a legal conclusion based on underlying factual findings and requires a case-by-case inquiry into the circumstances of disclosure. Public accessibility is the touchstone; the challenger bears the burden of proving public availability. Examples (Carella v. Starlight Archery) show that absence of evidence of public access defeats a 102(a) rejection. See In re Wyer, Kyocera, Blue Calypso, Medtronic, Klopfenstein and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic publications can qualify as 'printed publications' for prior-art purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic publications may be treated as 'printed publications' if they are publicly accessible to those of ordinary skill in the art exercising reasonable diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of electronic-publication status follows the same public-accessibility principles as for traditional printed publications. (Section heading begins discussion of electronic publications; examiners should apply the public accessibility tests similarly.)
